method: Compared contamination probes and adaptive reuse claims with Sainz et al., Deng et al., Dwork et al., and the OpenAI Realtime Eval Guide; recalculated historical answer-position counts and the exact Pearson-statistic multinomial tail from a versioned aggregate fixture under an explicitly assumed IID uniform-label null; executed the lesson's Python demo and ran eight offline assertions against prose, expected output, fixture integrity, and helper behavior. The fixture is a transcription of ignored local log summaries, not raw provider evidence. No provider calls or historical generation replay were performed.

observations.trace: Fixture batches report 20 generated / 20 parsed and 20 generated / 19 parsed; their analyzed A/B/C/D counts are 2/12/6/0 (n=20) and 2/14/3/0 (n=19). Exact conditional tail probabilities are approximately 0.0008710159 and 0.0000207091 under IID uniform labels. The lesson demo output matches its published text fence, including the corrected 19-to-10 literal fingerprint count; helper tests validate distribution arithmetic, input rejection, position rotation, and visible-corpus overlap candidates.

limitations: The historical prompts did not randomize answer positions; conditional tail probabilities are exploratory references, not evidence of a universal model preference or a valid pre-specified hypothesis test.
The 19-to-6 semantic grouping is a single human annotation without independent annotator agreement and cannot be generalized as a fixed generation defect rate.
Historical parser logs report only answer-field parseability (5/8, 19/20, 20/20), not complete schema validity, answer correctness, or item quality.

The original provider requests, model snapshot, complete scoring protocol, and reproducible raw responses are unavailable. The versioned fixture transcribes aggregate summaries from ignored local logs; its recorded source hashes identify those local files but do not authenticate provider output. This review does not replay the historical generation or prove/exclude training-data exposure.
Local n-gram matching only flags overlap candidates in accessible corpora; it cannot establish exposure to an unknown closed-model training corpus.
